We will obtain them for the right hon. gentleman. I did not bring [DOT]them downstairs. They are in Hansard of last session just as they were printed in the local paper, and I shall put them on Hansard as part of my observations in the exact terms in which they are quoted as the language of the right hon. gentleman. I do not desire
for a single moment to misquote him in that regard. The words as reported read:
There is one condition of that treaty which says that we are free to alter or to abrogate it altogether on six months' notice. I say to the farmers of Oxford that if the Australian treaty does any injury to your industry I will undertake to say on behalf of the government that I will give that six months' notice in short order.
But let us go a step further. How many members of this house supporting the Liberal party prior to 1921 and 1922 did not denounce the previous administration for governing by order in council? Have you ever heard of it? Is there one member of the government who has not gone through Canada and denounced .the Conservative administration for governing by order in council? And yet what have we here? We have a treaty which was not negotiated, we have a treaty which canid into being by order in council That is what I protest against now; I have always protested against it. I protest against any trade agreement which is made merely by order in council as a substitute for the collective will of the people as expressed in this parliament. The will of the cabinet is not sufficient. The cabinet at best is only the delegated authority or agent of this parliament and when it acts as such in respect to trade treaties it should not be permitted to function. In doing so it is going beyond its proper powers. I ask the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Crerar) what he thinks of making treaties by order in council? Where are those who in times gone by, my friend from South Huron (Mr. McMillan) and others, who talked so loudly of the mismanagement of the former administration, of their attempting to govern by orders in council; where are they now when a treaty with New Zealand is made by this government purely by order in council? Without negotiation, without discussion, without an opportunity for the members of this house to say whether they thought such an arrangement beneficial or otherwise, the government of the day passes an order in council and brings into being a trade treaty with New Zealand. The hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) the other day said it could not be described as a treaty. One of the sections of the Australian treaty made possible the passing of this order in council whereby the provisions of that trade agreement became applicable to New Zealand in its trade relations with this Dominion. It is true that section five of the Australian treaty was passed by this parliament. Of course it was. The government machinery was sufficiently powerful by a majority to enact it,

Australian Treaty-Mr. Bennett
and ifche division upon the passing of that treaty will be found in the journals of parliament, because that treaty was not adopted by this house without a vote. That treaty contained a clause which made possible the passing of this order in council. But I submit to this house and to the country that it is not sound parliamentary practice that an order in council should be the basis of a treaty. Always preceding any treaty there should 'be negotiations and discussions and opportunities to consider the various phases of the proposed agreement.
Hon. gentlemen this afternoon have argued that these treaties-the Australian treaty and its extension to New Zealand by order in council-have had no injurious effect upon	the dairy	industry of this	country.The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Millar) the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) and other hon. members have argued in that sense, that this treaty, called the New Zealand	'treaty, has had	no	injuriouseffect	upon the	dairy industry	of	Canada.Well,	I wonder	who, reading	the	records,
can seriously say that is so. We do know that before the treaty came into force, Canada was a country thait exported butter. We now know that it has ceased to be a country exporting butter in any quantity and has become a butter importing country in very large quantities from the Dominion with which the treaty was made; we know that 35,000,000 pounds of butter were brought last year from New Zealand, whence prior to that treaty little or none was imported, and we know that the markets we had in the countries of the world for the sale of our porducts are markets now satisfied by the products of other countries. Is there no cause and effect there? To what other cause is that change attributable? Is there any cause other than this treaty? Let that question be answered. Why is it you have your herds diminished by
125,000	milch cows? Is there any other cause? Previously to the treaty we had no importations, relatively, but we now have importations of about 35,000,000 pounds per annum and they are increasing.
In my hand I hold a copy of a Halifax paper, dated 6th of March, with these words contained therein:
Port Dunedin Smashes Record At Port Of Halifax
Motorship Is To Land Large Cargo Of Frozen Meats From Antipodes Port Dunedin's Cargo Includes 31,650 Carcasses of Lamb Has Butter Shipment Will Discharge 4.000 Quarters of Beef and 270 Bales of Wool
Smashing all re;ords at the port of Halifax for importations of frozen meats from the Antipodes, the Commonwealth and Dominion Line freighter Port Dunedin is due at eight o'clock this morning from Australian and New Zealand ports direct to land a total of 31,650 carcasses of lamb and 4,000 quarters of beef, according to an announcement made yesterday by the Robert Reford Company. The Port Dunedin is to discharge at pier 23.
In addition the freighter is to land 4,000 boxes of approximately 232.000 pounds of butter from New Zealand, and 270 bales of wool.
To Load Apples
Another feature of her visit is that the Port Dunedin will be the first ship of the Commonwealth and Dominion Line to load cargo at Halifax, a shipment of about 1,000 tons of freight including apples and general cargo, having been booked for the steamer. From Halifax, the Port Dunedin is to proceed to London.
Modern Freighter
One of the most modern freighters ever to visit the port the Dunedin is a motorship built in 1925. Her fuel-carrying capacity enabled her to sail from the Antipodes without replenishing her bunkers, and it is understood to take her across to England.
Her arrival follows 24 hours after the departure yesterday of the New Zealand Shipping Company's freighter Surrey which sailed yesterday for London after discharging nearly 110,000 boxes of New Zealand butter here.
Does this house realize that 110,000 boxes of butter means over 6.000,000 pounds, 3.000 tons? So that in one day 3,000 tons of New Zealand butter was landed in Halifax, and the next day 232.000 pounds more. Is that effect from the cause we have, indicated or not? We know that prior to this treaty the duty was 4 cents a pound on butter from New Zealand, and we now know it is 1 cent. We know that before this butter did not come. We now know it comes. Can a better case of cause and effect be mentioned than that? With respect to frozen mutton and frozen meats you have the same story. These are not fancies with respect to protein content in butter, or anything of the sort; these are facta established by the shipping records of the country. My hon. friend from Weyburn (Mr. Young) endeavours to say that a few men are promoting some purpose of their own.
I wonder if he realizes that in every part of Canada, in every province of Canada, the farmers have indicated that the result of this treaty is injurious to the dairy industry of the country.

May I say this to the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown), who spoke so feelingly about the use of the word "protection," and to my hon. friend from Weyburn (Mr. Young), and to my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar)-I think I can best illustrate the situation by referring to words that the hon. member for Lisgar should remember; I hope he has not forgotten them, although his associations during the last few years have not been conducive to his remembering. speechtext:
And all I can say with

I wiill not repeat the statements that have been made, indicating so clearly that the effects of the treaty are not limited to the dairy industry alone. You see them in the hog industry and the cattle industry; you see them reflected all the way along in our exports and in our imports. You see reflected the effects of this treaty. And so I say, sir, to the Prime Minister and to the members of his administration, that the difficulty with them in the negotiation of treaties is that they do not bring to bear upon the problems affected the consideration that their importance demands. They do not realize the implications of what they are doing. That has been the trouble. That was the difficulty with the French treaty, to which attention
has been drawn; that was the difficulty with the Italian treaty, and that is the difficulty with the New Zealand treaty. The government did not realize not only the direct results but the serious implications that followed from the course which they embarked upon, the logical consequences of their action.
But, sir, why are we arguing now about the value of this treaty, or what the government thinks about it? Do hon. gentlemen realize that the government itself now says that it proposes to substitute for the amendment which we have offered a subamendlment of its own, showing its lack of confidence in itself, by which they, in terms, declare that this treaty should be superseded? Why supersede what is a good thing? Will the hon. member for Lisgar bare his back and walk up to the punishment that is before him and say, I will now vote to supersede a treaty that I declare is good? Will the hon. member for Qu'Appelle walk up to the bench and vote for the superseding of the treaty which he says is good? Will he or will he not? Will the hon. member for Weyburn vote to supersede the treaty or not?

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY PROPOSED CANCELLATION OP SPECIAL AGREEMENT WITH NEW ZEALAND AND NEGOTIATION OP TREATY
speechtext:

will. He will march up to the sacrifice as they all do. Here are the words of the amendment. They are going to vote for a subamendment which will become an amendment to the motion to go into supply, and which will stand against supply being granted until it is disposed of. The amendment will then read:
That all the words after "be" in the fourth line of the amendment be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"That in the opinion of this house order in council No. 1557 passed on the 20th day of September, 1925, respecting certain trade arrangements with the Dominion of New Zealand be

Now here comes the subamendment. After the word "be," they are going to vote for whait?
-superseded as soon as possible by a treaty with that dominion and that immediate steps should be taken to negotiate such a treaty.
That is what they are going to vote for. It will be a spectacle for the gods to see them march up to the slaughter after they have declared that the treaty is one of the finest products of statesmanship the world has ever seen, after they have spoken all over the

country telling the people what a magnificent treaty it is, and how great the benefits are to this country. Now they are going to vote that it be superseded by a new treaty to be negotiated as soon as possible.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY PROPOSED CANCELLATION OP SPECIAL AGREEMENT WITH NEW ZEALAND AND NEGOTIATION OP TREATY
speechtext: That is a very intelligent answer, and it is for that reason we have proposed this amendment to the motion to go into supply. The Minister of Finance, who moved this house into supply, now suggests that he will supersede the New Zealand treaty with a new treaty to be negotiated as soon as possible. We have had some experience as to what the term "as soon as possible" means. We must remember that those words have a definite meaning on the part of the government, because only a few years ago the government was instructed to do something "as soon as possible." That was in 1926, and in 1930 they are moving. So if this government is permitted to remain in office and allowed to negotiate a treaty "as soon as possible," it may mean that action will be taken in the year 1934, and the hon. member, if he were then there, would start negotiations at that time. That is the reason we have asked that the order in council be rescinded forthwith; that is the reason we say that before any economic conference is held the great Dominion of New Zealand shall know exactly how Canadian sentiment stands. They should know that we are dissatisfied with this treaty, and desire a new treaty upon fair and equitable terms. We do not want any glittering platitudes to try to escape the responsibility that belongs to us; we desire to follow the good old course of saying "Clear the decks before you negotiate." give us an even chance and do not make this Dominon believe that this treaty will continue if we fail to arrive at a conclusion. Let me put this to the government: If you fail to negotiate a treaty, does this treaty stand or not? That is the question. Are you going to leave it there, or are you going to terminate it? Are you, Mr. Minister of Trade and Commerce, going to permit this treaty to remain or not? Does it stand, if your negotiations fail?

That is all I can say, yes. One of the largest dealers of this country asserted that he wanted to know where he stood in regard to these matters, because he did not like this government, Micawber-like, to be waiting for something to turn up. Commercial men make their contracts in advance so that they will know where they stand, and people who supply butter make contracts in advance so that they will know how those contracts will be filled. Mr. Speaker, we say that when two men begin to negotiate it is not good business for one to have his hands tied behind him.
The hon. member plays upon what he calls loyalty. All I can say is that the Conservative party always has stood before the people of this country and has said, " If you give a preference you should get one in return." That has been our policy since the days of Sir John A. Macdonald and Sir Charles Tup-per. As they pointed out, it always was competent for the Conservative party, when it was in power, to grant a jug-handled preference to any country if it so desired, but it said, " If we give we must get, and we do not propose to give the markets of our country to particular nations on a more favourable basis than we afford others unless we get something in return." That is the position we have taken, and when the Minister of Finance talks about loyalty, I say the greatest loyalty any man in this house owes is his loyalty to Canada rather than to any other country in the world, and he can best display that loyalty in this instance by seeing to it that the Canadian dairy producer gets an opportunity equal to that given the dairy producer in any other part of the world.
Tell me why the Canadian dairy farmer should lose his market to the extent of 35,000,000 pounds of butter per annum? Why should not that market be supplied by our own farmers? If we on this side of the house stand for the Canadian farmer it is because we believe our first duty to be to the Canadian people. We believe that the basic industry of this country is agriculture, and we believe that the dairy industry is one of the most important branches of agriculture. There has been a great deal of preaching about agricul-* ture going on throughout this country by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) who is not in his place, by those who come from the grain growing sections, and at times by the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Crerar) when he was not talking about something else. We have heard this preaching about the necessity of developing herds; we have heard about the thousands of dollars spent upon improving stock; we have heard about the increase in the quantity of milk and cream produced. When we think of these matters we believe them, and because we believe in them we propose to act upon our beliefs by abrogating an unfair and unjust trade agreement made by order in council between the Dominion of New Zealand and this country, which agreement does not afford to the Canadian farmer an equal opportunity with other producers to supply the requirements of his own people.
In times gone by, those who sit opposite to me have said it is cheap talk to speak about the British Empire and loyalty to that empire. That was the answer given by the Minister of Finance the other night as to why we should not abrogate the New Zealand treaty. He pictured this sister dominion of ours going to an economic conference after being hit between the eyes with the notice that this treaty is to be terminated. My experience, and the experience of men in this country who have had to deal with just such problems in days gone by at very vital moments in our history, has been that it is best to face facts squarely. We should say that New Zealand has nothing to expect from existing conditions; that we are going to start de novo; we are going to start on a different basis to negotiate a trade agreement on fair and equitable terms. By that we mean that unless we can do it in that way it will not be done. Let there be no misunderstanding about that. No agreement, Mr. Speaker, is fair or just or equitable which makes it possible to ship 35,000,000 pounds of butter into this country under a duty of one cent per pound while the freight rate on that butter in the refrigerator ships which bring it from New Zealand is only a little more per hundred pounds from New Zealand to Vancouver than the rate from Vancouver to Calgary by rail.

SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY PROPOSED CANCELLATION OP SPECIAL AGREEMENT WITH NEW ZEALAND AND NEGOTIATION OP TREATY
speechtext: moved the second reading of Bill No. 3, to amend the Navigable Waters Protection Act (approval of parliament.)

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY PROPOSED CANCELLATION OP SPECIAL AGREEMENT WITH NEW ZEALAND AND NEGOTIATION OP TREATY
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY PROPOSED CANCELLATION OP SPECIAL AGREEMENT WITH NEW ZEALAND AND NEGOTIATION OP TREATY
speechtext:
This is the same bill that was before the house last year. There was a division on the second reading, the yeas being 72 and the nays So. The Navigable Waters Protection Act was passed about 1909 when hydro-electric power development in Canada was practically in its infancy and the act was intended as a protection to the water powers and to help out the work of the International Deep Waterways Commission. Instead of the act fulfilling the function for which it was intended, it has not afforded any protection at all. There is in Canada hardly a navigable stream where they have not given away the water powers. The absurd construction placed upon the act in many places throughout the country has almost brought the act into ridicule. I will refer in a moment or two to the decisions regarding the Humber river.
The bill now before the house proposes to restore the approval power to parliament and to remove it from the Minister of Public Works. It amends chapter 140 of the revised statutes of Canada, which is a general statute known as the Navigable Waters Protection Act 1909. It provides that the jurisdiction now vested in the Minister of Public Works shall be repealed in so far as it affects international navigable boundary waters.
The first clause of the bill provides that the following shall be inserted immediately after section nine of the said act:
9A (1) No work except harbour improvements shall be commenced or constructed in, upon, over, under, through or across any international navigable boundary waters between the Dominion of Canada and the United States of America, or any part of the river St. Lawrence-
The house will notice that this is limited* to international navigable boundary waters between Canada and the United States.
-without the approval of parliament or on any terms or conditions other than those approved by parliament.
Clause (2) of the proposed bill provides:
Plans of any such work, in duplicate, and a description of the proposed site, shall be deposited with the Clerk of the House of Commons.
Clause (3) provides:
No order in council, regulation or permit purporting to grant the right to commence or construct such work shall have any force or effect unless authorized by parliament.
The last clause provides:
The preceding section shall be deemed to have come into force on the 1st day of January, 1930.
In the Navigable Waters Protection Act there is a definition of word "work". What is "work" under the act? It is as follows:
"Work" includes any bridge, boom, dam, aboiteau, wharf, dock, pier or other structure, tunnel or pipe, or telegraph or power cable or wire and the approaches or other works necessary or appurtenant thereto, or any work, structure or device, whether similar in character to the foregoing or not, which may interfere with navigation.
A great principle of public policy is involved in this bill. As the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. McRae) said last year in a similar debate on the Seven Sisters power matter, the exploitation of water power in the United States is the crime of the century. That was also the opinion of President Roosevelt and it is the opinion of everybody who has the public interest at heart. It is a crime to throw away all these magnificent water powers to private greed and gain when they are needed for navigation purposes. Navigation seems to be made a football of in the house. When you hear people talking about water power, you would think there were only two provinces in confederation. Take for instance the St. Lawrence waterways. If the Dominion government would develop the power and have a national hydro-electric power policy for this country, and develop and generate power from canal works and sell it at cost, what they would make out of it would pay for the St. Lawrence waterway, but they are giving this power away to the provinces. One province has given away the Beauharnois power. Another company is to be given power in the Ottawa river at the Carillon falls and another private company, the St. Maurice. Three years ago the government were committed to giving the Carillon away also. At that time the government could not lay down a policy. I asked the Minister of Railways and Canals: Will you lay down a policy regarding the Carillon power, and he did not do so until some time afterwards when the



Navigable Waters-Mr. Church
people rose against it. As regards the Seven Sisters, they called a conference and the result of it was that they gave away the Seven Sisters falls to a lot of private capitalists and also the Beauharnois. The units of Beau-harnois stock rose from ten, and one hundred dollars and now are one thousand dollars.
Where does the high court of parliament come in as regards this act? In Ontario there is an act that provides that no municipality can give away a franchise without the vote of the electorate. That act was placed on the statute books by Sir James Whitney. I would repeal the Beauharnois contract under the powers contained in the Navigatble Waters Act because the act provides for that being done. They have not kept their contract so far no money has been spent on navigation. The question was debated in the Quebec legislature a short time ago and some of the members described the Beauharnois people as one of the most gigantic trusts and monopolies on the north American continent today. It was urged in the Quebec legislature last week that it should be repealed. I would repeal it to-day. It would be good Conservative doctrine if you did appeal it.
In 1905 Sir James Whitney and Sir Adam Beck criticized the Ross government for giving away the whole Niagara river to Mackenzie and Mann and other power interests. An election took place in 1905 and the municipalities rose in rebellion. There was a change of government and Sir James Whitney came into office. Within twenty four hours he revoked that contract and restored that river for all time to the people of Ontario. Private ownership was bought out, in some cases given thirty three and a third per cent and in some cases fifty per cent more was given them to get out, and they got out gradually and the Niagara was finally restored to the people. What happened in the Niagara river yesterday will happen in the St. Lawrence to-day if there was any public spirit in Ontario. What will posterity say when they sail up the St. Lawrence and see what is happening on that river, this handing over of those magnificent resources over the heads of the people? The people have had nothing to say about the matter at all. They are sold into power slavery to these power companies. The people's representatives are also powerless and can do nothing because of this antiquated 1909 act; they cannot say anything because of this act which is one of the most monstrous acts for giving away to private companies the title deeds to our natural resources. It is called the Navigable Waters Protection Act. There is no "protection" whatever about it.

The people are not protected. It protects power barons A, B and C in getting away with the title deeds to power not only in the St. Lawrence but in many other streams.
Now is the time for parliament to assert itself if there is any respect for public rights in Canada. It would1 have paid the province of Ontario to have gone ahead with the development of power at Morrisburg. The water flows past Ontario's door on the way to Quebec, and Ontario has the first claim to it. Sir Adam Beck asked for power under this particular act to develop and generate it at Morrisburg, and to erect a dam on the St. Lawrence, there to generate power for the province of Ontario. But what was the minister's reply? He would not empower him to do it, but gave Quebec the power refused Ontario, for the Beauharnois people, thus making Ontario just a filling station for the Quebec power privately owned. Ontario should have insisted on the Morrisburg dam. The Dominion government has been sacrificing the rights and privileges of the people of this country. I say that it would be both good politics and good policy for hon. gentlemen opposite to develop these magnificent water-powers and preserve them for all posterity. Let us launch a great national hydro policy and develop and generate that power, to protect the people from the exorbitant rates which will otherwise be charged both for the Gatineau power and the Beauharnois power in the years that are to come. The people of the province of Ontario will pay in charges for direct current sufficient to retire the whole of the bonds in thirty years. What will be the result at the end of that thirty-year term? Instead of quoting S15 per horse-power as they do to-day, which is too much already, they will want $40, $50, $60 or $70 per horse-power, and it will serve Ontario right. Where is the Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan), who poses as the friend of the workingmen? I see that he has gone to open a Liberal campaign in the city of London. What is he doing to save these water-power resources to the workingman?

Last session I asked the minister who were the directors and president of the Beauhairnois, and the reply I received was: "No information." Imagine, no information as to who the party of the first pant was, as to their bona fides, as to their ability to carry out the work. I pointed out then, and I repeat now, that the order in council is ultra vires of this parliament because that work interferes with the flow of the water from the great lakes to the sea. This country settled its canal policy in 1854 for all time. This country, since 1854, has jurisdiction over all canals and operates them as national undertakings, as links in the transportation system; but last year the government made a scrap of paper of this long settled canal policy by letting the Beauharnois contract, giving 'these people the right to build, among other things, a navigation canal. The government is going to build the locks itself. What is the government going to get out of it? These people are changing the bed of the river. They are erecting big weirs, which may fall down, and some of the municipalities in Ontario are holding meetings about it. The time has come for parliament to assert itself before it is too late. So this is Liberalism as they have it up to date! That is the way Liberalism parts with the natural resources of this country, with the Seven Sisters power site, with Beauharnois, the Gatineau, and other sites. That might have been all right thirty yeans ago, giving aiway water-powers to .private capitalists, but that policy was stopped in Ontario long ago by Sir James Whitney. This government will have the battle of its life 'before many years are over for having alienated the water-powers of the St. Lawrence. The water-powers are the property of the people. I am sorry to see Sir Adam Beck's work being undone.
Only the other day the municipality of Toronto sent a deputation down here with reference to a bridge over the Humber. The deputation was met by five cabinet ministers, who talked more that morning than they have done all session in the house. One of the matters discussed was the erection of a bridge across the Humber river, a little stream where water lilies grow, and 'canoes and row boats and other small craft ply about. The minister contended that that was a navigable stream. Three hundred thousand Shriners are coming to Canada, and I would suggest that the minister mobilize the Canadian navy on the Humber and give a demonstration to the American people of what the department can do. That just shows the absurdity to which the act can be carried. It puts me in mind of the fifth proposition in Euclid, the pons 2410-32i
asinorum, the absurdity to which the minister is prepared to go in interpreting that act. On a Sunday two thousand motor cars will be waiting to cross over that small bridge. There are many bridges across the river mow. There is first the electric railway bridge. There is a vehicular bridge, and I would suggest that my hon. friend from Southeast Grey, if she were there on a Sunday, could do a good business removing people's tonsils while they are waiting to cross. The case of the Humber was settled in 1909 by Mr. Pugsley, when he was Minister of Public Works. I might point out that farther up the river some of the municipalities are asking for a bridge and the township of York is encouraging them. In spite of all the traffic that crosses the Humber, the minister says that we will have to have a swing bridge. This bridge that we are asking for over the Humber is necessary, and it could have been completed before summer if it had not been for the absurd way in which this particular application has been treated. If this is what the new Liberalism means, all I can say is that there will be a day of reckoning.
Talk of the family compact of 1837! It was a mere myth compared with the family compact that we have to-day-a family compact that has grabbed the water-powers from the people, grabbed them over the heads ol the representatives of the people in parliament assembled. The representatives of the people have nothing to say; they stand in the side lines while the family compact go ahead with their schemes. These exploiters of the public domain are in many cases Americans. Who own the Beauharnois power rights? Who are the directors of that company and of other similar power companies? Last year the federal trade commission of the United States investigated the activities of the power trusts of that country, and the sworn evidence adduced before that commission showed that these power interests in the United States were buying up newspapers and had established a great super power trust, reaching from the city of Washington up to Boston and New York and then over into Canada. Already they have grabbed many of our best water-powers. The Navigable Waters Protection Act has outlined its usefulness, although originally intended as a protective measure to assist the International Joint Commission. Its main purpose was to conserve for future generations our water-powers instead of giving them to private corporations for exploitation. The power barons are flourishing in this country like the proverbial green bay tree. Who is going to stop their activities? The power to

Navigable Waters-Mr. Elliott
do so has been taken away from the representatives of the people here assembled. Are we going to stand for that? Or are we going to assert the interests of the people? I am glad to see that the Progressive party in the west have for many years been alive to this situation, and showed it by the fight they made against the alienation of the Seven Sisters water-power. I hope before the evening is over they will assert themselves on this question in the interests of the people of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as my hon. friend from Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church) has said, this is a bill which was rejected by this house last session. The main reasons given by him in its favour on that occasion were that if adopted it would have the effect of revoking the approval given to the plans of the Beau-harnois Company. Apparently he has changed his view with regard to that company in the meantime, because the bill which he now introduces is to be deemed to have come into force on the first day of January, 1930, so that it would not operate to revoke the permit given to the Beauharnois Company.
In regard to the application of the city of Toronto to construct a bridge over the Humber river, which he described as not being a navigable river, may I refer my hon. friend to the fact that the city-of which I think he was then solicitor, if not mayor at the time- when an application was made by the Canadian National Railways, formerly the Grand Trunk, for approval of plans of a bridge across that river, opposed the application on the ground that the Humber was a navigable river. That was the attitude of the city of Toronto some years ago.
I do not propose to enter into an argument with my hon. friend as to whether the attitude taken by the department in regard to the approval of plans for a bridge to be constructed by the city of Toronto over the Humber river is correct or not. All I have to say that that is the attitude which has been taken by the department in regard to these various applications ever since 1882, when the Navigable Waters Protection Act came into force. Under that legislation, which is very simple, if an application is made for approval of plans it is addressed to the Public Works Department, and in this connection may I call the attention of the house to the following clause:
No work shall be built or placed in, upon, over, under, through or across any navigable water unless the site thereof has been approved by the governor in council, nor unless such work is built, placed and maintained in accordance with plans and regulations approved or made by the governor in council.
IMf. Church.]
What is primarly the object of this clause? It is to ascertain that the site selected for the proposed structure is the proper site. That, as I say, is the primary object; after that come the details or plans providing for the structure. When an application of this kind has been made it is advertised for four weeks in the Canada Gazette and in two local newspapers, so as to give notice to anybody who may desire to object to the proposed structure. If any serious objection is raised, it is the practice for the Minister of the department to give a hearing at which in the presence of the Departmental engineers all parties concerned -may appear and present their views.
May I call -attention to the kind of thing done under this act? After listening to what I have to say I think my hon. friend will be one of the first to see what the effect of his bill would be. In 1927 the department approved of seventy-six applications, in 1928 of eighty-three, and in 1929 of eighty-five. Under his bill, as drawn, not -all such applications would require to be confirmed by private acts of parliament, but the great majority of them would. Of local private acts, in 1927 we had thirty-six, in 1928 twenty-nine, and in 1929 thirty-four. So if my hon. friend's suggestion were adopted we would about treble the number of local private acts required -to be passed on by this house.
Now, what are the things that my hon. friend would have dealt with by this parliament? I may give a few instances. A short time ago we were called upon to approve the transmission line of the Niagara Power Company across -the Niagara river. The main question was as to whether the transmission lines were in the opinion of the engineers satisfactory. Another application was as to the proper location of the Bell Telephone cable from Prescott to Ogdensburg. The main question involved -there was as to whether or not it was placed low enough, and as to whether or not the site was correct. Another application had reference to the Bell Telephone cable to Port Huron, Michigan. The question there was as to whether it was placed far enough under where -the boats were travelling to make navigation safe. Another application was the -location of a proposed oil pipe of the Imperial Oil Company between Sarnia and Port Huron. The question there was a3 to whether the location was proper.
Those are samples of what would, under my hon. friend's bill, require acts of parliament. There is a clear distinction, which my hon. friend, as an excellent municipal -lawyer, knows very well, between the acts that are done as legislative acts and those that are done as administrative acts.

Navigable Waters-Mr. Elliott
So far as the right to cross a river with a cable is concerned, the Navigable Waters Protection Act has for nearly fifty years permitted that right, provided the cable was properly located and so constructed as to protect navigation. But the administrative act which is performed by engineers after investigation is as to W'hether the site is correct, whether it is at the proper depth or height, and whether all the possible safeguards to navigation have been provided.
I submit that it would very greatly increase the work of this house, and perhaps, in some cases, double the length of the session, if these things were done by this legislative body rather than by an administrative departmental body. They are technical questions. Engineering expert opinions have to govern in regard to them. This parliament, for instance, would not go to Sarnia to see whether the site of the oil pipe of the Imperial Oil Company for transmitting oil from Sarnia to Port Huron was or was not in the proper place. An engineer would do it, just as an engineer does it now'. The suggestion of my hon. friend is wholly impracticable. May I also point out that it is now, and has been for nearly half a century, absolutely unnecessary, because if it is the public that he wishes to protect against something improper being done, under the Navigable Waters Protection Act they are now protected by section 12, which says:
Parliament may, at any time, annul or vary any order of the governor in council made under this part. Any action of parliament in that behalf shall not be deemed an infringement of the rights of the local authority, company or person concerned.
They are not limited. After the approval is granted they may, at any time, annul or vary any order of the governor in council made under this part. The public, therefore, are absolutely protected by section 12 of the act, and the act as it now stands is a practical, well-working act, which gives rise to very little difficulty. It has worked out well through all the time it has been in operation.
I cannot agree with the bill as proposed. It would largely cumber the records of the house; as I say, it would probably double the length of the session, and would not meet the requirements of the various concerns which are seeking development in this country. Suppose some concern comes along and desires approval of a pipe line, or something of that kind, from Prescott to Ogdensburg, or from Sarnia to Port Huron, just after the close of the session; all their development, all their business would be held up until the following year. I am sure that that would not be the desire of hon. members of this house. As my hon. friend
the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) reminds me, under section 12 parliament can always review, repeal or annul whatever has been done under this act.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY PROPOSED CANCELLATION OF SPECIAL AGREEMENT WITH NEW ZEALAND AND NEGOTIATION OF TREATY.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the
hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) in justifying his amendment to the motion to go into supply by which he called for the immediate cancellation of the Dominion s trade agreement with the sister dominon ot New Zealand, prefaced his remarks with the statement that the government had failed to realize the serious condition of the agricultural industry. He then cited the circular which was sent out by the Department of Agriculture calling the attention of the producers of Canada to the fact that there had been a serious decline in agricultural exports. The hon. member interpreted the circular to mean that the industry was not in a good position because the exports were declining, but he is quite mistaken in the intention of the circular sent out by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell). The circular was an appeal to the agriculturists of Canada to
the effect that if they wanted to hold their place in the export market, certain branches of industrial production would have to be speeded up; it did not in any way indicate the inference put upon it by my hon. friend.
The hon. member then went on to say that the farmers of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec were beginning to realize that the greatest asset which agriculture had was the home market, and that this market was especially valuable to the producers of butter, but he did not refer in any way to the value of the home market created by the export from this Dominion to sister dominions of S40,-000,000 worth of processed merchandise. The criticism of the hon. member was based largely upon what he termed the neglect by this government of the dairy industry, and he based his argument upon the extent of the importation of butter.
I want to make a statement clearly, without prejudice and without bias, and I will state the situation in the dairy industry as it appeals to me, using figures which are authoritative, which I do not think can be contradicted and which I believe other hon. members have used. Admittedly there has been a substantial increase in the importation of butter from Australia and New Zealand, which importation amounted to approximately
35,000,000 pounds during the past year. Thirty-five million pounds of butter is exactly 12J per cent of the total consumption of butter in this Dominion, so that it can be stated quite fairly that out of every 8 pounds of butter consumed in the Dominion, 7 pounds were produced within our boundaries, and 1 pound was produced in New Zealand.
Likewise during the period under review there has been a substantial increase in the exports from Canada amounting to $40,000,000. For quite some time there has been a decided interest on the part of Canadians in the Australian and New Zealand trade. This interest is evidenced on every hand, but it is best evidenced by the fact that the Department of Trade and Commerce, since these treaties went into effect, has received more than 200 and, in fact, I think almost 300 letters from various producers in the dominion who, at the time the treaties went into effect, were not interested in export but who, since the treaties have been in existence, have become interested. These producers have approached the government with the request that we should enter into negotiations to have a broadening of the terms of the treaty so that the favourable relations might be extended to more commodities than were considered at the time the treaty was made.

It is also true that representations had been made to the government by those interested in the dairy industry. From time to time representatives of the dairy industry have claimed that the preference given to New Zealand butter was altogether too great and we have been asked by the dairy industry to enter into negotiations with the two governments so that the terms of the treaty might be modified or a new treaty might be made.
Another point I wish to make with regard to these treaties is that since the inauguration of the direct steamship service between Vancouver and New Zealand in the last year, our exports of lumber to Australia have more than doubled. They were falling off very much in the fiscal year ending March 31, 1929, but during the last six months of 1929 our exports of lumber from British Columiba to the Antipodes have more than doubled. Indeed at this very moment there is in Australia and New Zealand a deputation of Canadian lumbermen canvassing the situation there and cabling the government to enter into negotiations with a view of hawing better tariffs arranged on Canadian lumber entering Australia and New Zealand.
These are not the only arguments which have brought about the condition which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) has described. When the treaty was entered into with Australia and afterwards extended by order in council to New Zealand, the exchange was not in exadtly the same position that it is in to-d!ay. Cables from London indicate that New Zealand money is to-day at a discount of four per cent-yesterday it was three per cent-so that many new factors have entered into the question. The government has concluded that, as the conditions existing in Canada during the past yeai under this treaty were not as favourable in some respects as they had been, and as there is a still greater possiblity of extending ouir trade to those dominions, providing for certain commodities which we now know we can export but which in 1925 we did not know we could export, very careful study should be given to the terms of the treaty, the opportunities for further export and to the representations of the dairy council with regard to the importation of butter.
These considerations have brought about certain negotiations which have been conducted by our trade commissioner, Mr. Croft, in New Zealand with the government of New Zealand, representing to that government that Canada actually desired a cessation of the
[Mi. Malcolm.]
operations under which we are now working and desired to make a new trade treaty directly with that sister dominion.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), when he was speaking, laid great stress on one or two points. Particularly he directed my attention to the position we would be in should the order in council which extends the terms of the Australian treaty to New Zealand not be cancelled. While I am dealing with that I should like to point out that the criticism of my hon. friend as to the government making a treaty by order in council is not well founded. When the Australian treaty was before the house for discussion, every hon. member then present knows that clause 5 of the treaty read:
Subject to the provisions of the customs tariff, 1907, the governor in council may, by order in council, extend the said advantages to goods the produce or manufacture of-
Not New Zealand, but "any British country."
In approving the principle of the Australian treaty, the Canadian parliament by a substantial majority gave the government authority to extend the same privileges to any other British country. If hon. members had so objected to those privileges being extended by order in council, I do not think they could have done other than have spoken and voted against the adoption of the Australian treaty, or at least voted for the removal of the objectionable clause. The Minister of Finance has stated to the house that these representations have been made. Therefore I think it is largely a matter of form as to how they should be made. The amendment of the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) calls for an immediate cancellation of the order in council and the opening up of negotiations between the sister dominion of New Zealand and Canada. The subamendment states that, negotiations having been entered into, negotiations should continue without cancellation of the order in council.
May I call my hon. friend's attention to one or two points which must be considered? As the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) stated to-day, we could not immediately stop the importation of anything from New Zealand because the terms of the Australian treaty, which terms were extended to New Zealand, demand that six months' notice be given. Therefore even if we gave notice, it would be six months before the notice could be effective. My hon. friend says that he wants to start with a clean sheet, to wipe out past arrangements, before he starts to

Australian Treaty-Mr. Malcolm
negotiate. In as large projects as this, where contracts have been in existence, I believe he himself has negotiated for new terms of contract without cancelling the old. Every businessman in Canada has done the same thing. Within less than six months we are facing an economic conference and if negotiations can be carried on in the interim, over the thousands of miles that intervene between this Dominion and New Zealand, it is quite possible that the economic conference will provide the best place for a full discussion of our differences. I feel sure that a treaty can be drafted without any difficulty to supplement the order in council.
As much has been said against the benefits of the treaty by the leader of the opposition and other members, I should like to refer to the results of these treaties. One cannot treat our trade relations between the two dominions separately, as the same terms apply in each in relation to imports.

As a result there is practically no importation of butter from Australia. The importation is almost all from New Zealand; it is relatively small from Australia.
But before I go into that, I want to refer to the remarks of my hon. friend. My hon. friend used the most extravagant language of which he is capable-and that means the most extravagant language there is-in speaking of the dairy industry. My hon. friend told the house of the deplorable condition of the dairy industry. The facts as related by hon. gentlemen opposite as to the condition of the dairy industry are not borne out by the statements of those engaged in the industry. I should like to read the most authoritative statement that I believe can be read to the Canadian house of parliament. The Ontario Milk Producer is a journal which is supposed to be looking after the interests of the dairy men of the province, just as the government considers that it is looking after the interests of the milk producers who are the farmers of the Dominion. This is not an old issue of the Ontario Milk Producer, but the March issue of 1930, and the leading editorial has this to say:
Nineteen-thirty should be the producer's year. In saying this we have no thought of prices in mind. No one can forecast prices with any great degree of accuracy. We can vouch for this however. Prices for dairy products generally at this, the beginning of another production season, are at least as high in Canada as in any other dairy country we know of. And this applies to manufactured products such as butter and cheese, more particularly the farmer. In so far as values are concerned the dairymen of Canada start off in 1930 on a pretty good footing as compared with the dairymen of some other countries.
I think we will all agree that the hon. leader of the opposition made a very telling election speech. It should appeal to anybody in the country who conceded his premises. My hon. friend is a very astute and clever debater. He has spent his whole life in trying to make good cases out of mighty bad ones. He is as able a lawyer and as able a debater as the British Empire has ever had. I will pay him the compliment of saying that he is able to make a better case out of a bad case than any other man who has been in this house.
Now I want to give the actual figures. In
1925 our imports were:
From Australia	$ 2,271,216
From New Zealand. . . .	1,713,830
Total of	$ 3,985,046
In the year 1929 our total imports were:
From Australia	$ 3,519,123
From New Zealand. . . .	14,987,302
Total of	$18,506,425
In return, see how our export trade to these countries has grown. In the year 1925, our exports were:
To Australia	$14,061,658
To New Zealand	 16,213,942
Total of	$30,275,600
In the year 1929, our exports were:
To Australia	$19,135,217
To New Zealand	 20,424,710
Total of	$39,559,927
A customer that gives us $40,000,000 worth of business in return for $18,000,000 worth is a customer worth considering, and at this time in the economic history of the world, when every economist of note is pointing out that world trade and export trade are the fundamentals of success for every nation, when we are endeavouring to market our products in every country in ever increasing quantities, when we have succeeded in build-

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY PROPOSED CANCELLATION OF SPECIAL AGREEMENT WITH NEW ZEALAND AND NEGOTIATION OF TREATY.
speechtext: The figures in the pamphlet issued by the hon. gentleman's department show a diminution in the number of milch cows between 1927 and 1928 of 101,000, and 6,000 certain in 1929.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY PROPOSED CANCELLATION OF SPECIAL AGREEMENT WITH NEW ZEALAND AND NEGOTIATION OF TREATY.
speechtext:
My hon. friend may be quite correct, but a small percentage like that would not affect the matter at all because we are dealing in very large figures.
The dairy herds of Canada, I believe it 13 safe to say, have not varied in any one year between 1925 and 1928 by 100,000. In 1925 our dairy herds comprised 3,200,000 cattle. In 1927 the figure might have been slightly higher than in 1928.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY PROPOSED CANCELLATION OF SPECIAL AGREEMENT WITH NEW ZEALAND AND NEGOTIATION OF TREATY.
speechtext: Higher by 101,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY PROPOSED CANCELLATION OF SPECIAL AGREEMENT WITH NEW ZEALAND AND NEGOTIATION OF TREATY.
speechtext:
It may be that as to 1929 my hon. friends are correct because there had been a heavy sale of milch cattle to the United States, but in no one year has the total number of 3,200,000 cattle diminished by 100,000, and that is a small percentage.
There has been an increase of 126,000,000 pounds of milk produced on the farms of this country between 1925 and 1928. It is only fair to say that the manufacture of butter and cheese in this Dominion has slightly decreased. In 1925 we produced 269,495,000 [Mf. Malcolm.]
pounds of butter, and in 1928, 258,027,000 pounds, or a decline of 11,468,000 pounds, being 4 per cent. In the manufacture of cheese we had a larger decline. In 1925 we produced 177,672,000 pounds of cheese; in 1928, 145,019,000 pounds, or a decline of
32.653.000.	That is a decline, I will admit, of 20 per cent.
The total estimated consumption of butter rose from 256,000,000 pounds in 1925, to 280,000,000 pounds in 1928, an increase of nearly
24.000.	000 pounds in four years. The per capita consumption of butter rose during the same period from 23.61 pounds per person to 29.06 pounds, which indicates, I contend, a very distinct rise in the standard of living of the Canadian people.
As a result of this lack of increase in production and the decided increase in consumption, Canada for the last few years has been on basis, an importer of butter. In 1928 our imports exceeded our exports by nearly 15,000,000 pounds, whereas in 1925 our exports exceeded our imports by 26,000,000 pounds. In the calendar year just closed we imported
35,928,000	pounds of butter and exported
1.404.000,	leaving us an importer, on balance, of 34,500,000 pounds.
Offsetting these two declines in the production of butter and cheese we have two gains, one a gain of 34,000,000 pounds of milk used in the manufacture of condensed milk, powdered milk and other products, and the other a gain in the consumption of fresh milk by our people of 718,000,000 pounds. The value of the total dairy production of this Dominion is what counts, and that has not declined, the figures for 1928 being slightly higher than for any previous year.
While the value of creamery butter produced w'as about $1,000,000 less in 1928 than in 1927, on the other hand the value of the cheese production was $5,000,000 more in 1928 than in 1927. The selling value of the dairy and creamery butter in Canada in 1925 was $95,000,000, and in 1928, $93,000,000, although the quantity was 11,000,000 pounds less. The value of the cheese production in Canada in 1925 was $36,500,000. The value declined in 1928 by $5,000,000 to $30,500,000, Although the decline in the actual number of pounds produced was 32,000,000. The total value of milk production in this country-and it is the total value of the milk production that is of the greatest interest to the farmers-in the year 1925 was $284,000,000, and in 1928, $297,000,000, or a gain of $13,000,000.
I want to refer to a subject to which some hon. gentlemen speaking from the other side of the house made reference a few evenings ago. I want to ask any member whether he

thinks he has the right to dictate to the producer of milk how he shall sell his milk. In some counties the milk producers receive a very much higher price for their milk sold in the form of cream; in other counties they receive their best price from the condensed milk factories; and in some locations near large cities they receive their best price by selling their milk fresh to the dairies. If our farmers, for other reasons, are not particularly attracted by the laborious work of operating a dairy and choose to take the easier course of selling their milk in the fresh form, I do not see that it is the duty of any member of this house to dictate to them as to what manufacturing industry they shall sell their product. I would say to my hon. friend the leader of the opposition that one might just as well argue on behalf of the lumber industry as against the pulp and paper industry. If a man can get a higher price for his spruce logs from the pulp mill than from the saw mill, then it is his privilege to sell to the pulp mill rather than to the saw mill.
The production of butter for 1929 is as yet unknown, but it is interesting to note that our butter imports exceeded our butter exports by 34,500,000 pounds, and as the stocks in cold storage were comparable with those for the preceding year, it is safe to assume the consumption of butter in Canada exceeded production by something like 34,500,000 pounds.
Let us analyse our production and consumption in conjunction with the export figures. We have an excess consumption of 24,000,000 pounds by our own calculation. We also have by our own calculation a decrease in production of 11,000,000 pounds. Those figures total 35,000,000 pounds. So the calculation of our butter imports and exports must be correct, and we must be short of reaching our consumption within this Dominion by our own production by something like this amount quoted of 35,000,000 pounds.
Now, it may be argued that the price paid for butter in the Dominion was not sufficiently high during the period to induce our farmers to make enough butter to meet the home demand. But if this argument be true, it equally holds true for export and explains why our farmers did not wish to make butter for the export market, because in the Dominion during the past few years the prevailing price for butter has been from three to four cents a pound higher than the price on the Liverpool market, to which our export butter was shipped. In 1928 the average price in Montreal was 40-66 cents; in Liverpool it was 37-05 cents. In 1929 the average price in Montreal was 42-09 cents; in Liverpool it
Australian Treaty-Mr. Malcolm
was 38-03 cents. Indeed, sir, at the very moment the prevailing prices for butter are higher in the Dominion than they are in England or the United States.
Now, let us admit, just for the sake of being agreeable to my hon. friends opposite, that their argument is correct, that the home market is the best market for the Canadian milk producer who sells his product, not in the form of fresh milk, not to the condensing plant, but to the dairy factory. Compare the present conditions of the milk producer with the conditions existing when this government took the reins of office in 1922. Then the home market would not consume the butter produced, and we were on an export price basis, the export price governed the returns of the milk producer. In 1922 the milk producers of this Dominion were paid by the dairy factories for their milk the enormous sum of $76,477,000. But something happened in the meantime. A great home market sprang up; an increase in the consumption of butter running into tens of millions of pounds took place. By 1928 the home production could not supply the domestic demand, and there being no export, home prices governed-prices from three to four cents higher than could have been obtained if export prices had governed. As a consequence during that year, 1928, the men for whom we are thinking, these men whose interests have been so sadly neglected by this government-as my hon. friend says- these men were paid by the dairy factories for their milk not $76,000,000 but $103,000,000. The milk producers of this country, for whose interests my hon. friends opposite are so concerned, received for their milk $27,000,000 more from the dairy factories in 1928 than they did in 1922.
Nothing has been said by my hon. friends opposite as to our increasing consumption of fresh milk at better prices than the dairy factories pay; nothing has been said of the export of cream and milk to the United States amounting to sufficient to make 25,000,000 pounds of butter. Had this not been exported, had it been made into butter in Canada, to-day we would be, not on an import basis, but an export basis, and instead of home prices governing our milk producers would be taking export prices for their product. If the dairy farmer can export his products more profitably in the form of milk and cream than in the form of butter, who is going to gainsay his right to do so?
Now, we are speaking of giving consideration to the dairy industry. There is more than one way of helping the industry. A few years ago we were told by hon. gentlemen

Australian Treaty-Mr. Malcolm
opposite that this government was giving too much consideration to agriculture and very little consideration to the manufacturing industry.

speechtext: Who said that?

speechtext:
That was the general
argument from the other side of the house.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY PROPOSED CANCELLATION OF SPECIAL AGREEMENT WITH NEW ZEALAND AND NEGOTIATION OF TREATY.
speechtext: It never was.
